original_value: Just-in-time software defect prediction (JIT-SDP) is an active topic in software defect prediction, which aims to identify defect-inducing changes. Recently, some studies have found that the variability of defect data sets can affect the performance of defect predictors. By using local models, it can help improve the performance of prediction models. However, previous studies have focused on module-level defect prediction. Whether local models are still valid in the context of JIT-SDP is an important issue. To this end, we compare the performance of local and global models through a large-scale empirical study based on six open-source projects with 227417 changes. The experiment considers three evaluation scenarios of cross-validation, cross-project-validation, and timewise-cross-validation. To build local models, the experiment uses the k-medoids to divide the training set into several homogeneous regions. In addition, logistic regression and effort-aware linear regression (EALR) are used to build classification models and effort-aware prediction models, respectively. The empirical results show that local models perform worse than global models in the classification performance. However, local models have significantly better effort-aware prediction performance than global models in the cross-validation and cross-project-validation scenarios. Particularly, when the number of clusters k is set to 2, local models can obtain optimal effort-aware prediction performance. Therefore, local models are promising for effort-aware JIT-SDP.

result.paraphrase: Just-in-time software defect prediction (JIT-SDP) is an active research area in software defect prediction, aiming to identify changes that induce defects. Recent studies have shown that variability in defect datasets can influence defect predictor performance, and local models may improve prediction results. However, prior work has mainly examined module-level defect prediction, so it remains an important question whether local models are still effective in the JIT-SDP setting. To address this, we conducted a large-scale empirical study comparing local and global models across six open-source projects and 227417 changes. The experiments evaluated three scenarios: cross-validation, cross-project-validation, and timewise-cross-validation. For local models, k-medoids was used to partition the training set into multiple homogeneous regions. Logistic regression and effort-aware linear regression (EALR) were then employed to construct classification and effort-aware prediction models, respectively. The empirical findings indicate that local models underperform global models in classification, but significantly outperform them in effort-aware prediction under the cross-validation and cross-project-validation scenarios. In particular, setting the number of clusters k to 2 yields the best effort-aware prediction performance. Thus, local models appear promising for effort-aware JIT-SDP.
